flashcards.q: The four decisions made before any sample-size arithmetic?
flashcards.a: (1) OEC + 2-4 guardrails declared in writing; (2) randomization unit (user/session/cluster); (3) MDE priced from ship-AND-maintain economics (AI features include inference COGS); (4) direction and duration - >=2 full weekly cycles.

flashcards.q: Sample size for baseline 5%, +10% relative MDE, alpha .05 two-sided, power .8?
flashcards.a: n/arm = (1.96+0.84)^2 x [0.05x0.95 + 0.055x0.945] / 0.005^2 ~= 31,205 per arm (~62,400 total). At 8K eligible users/day that's ~8 days -> schedule ~14-15 to cover two weekly cycles.

flashcards.q: State the three scaling laws of the power formula.
flashcards.a: Halve MDE -> ~4x sample (effect is squared in denominator); 80%->90% power -> ~1.34x n ((1.96+1.28)^2/(1.96+0.84)^2 ~= 10.5/7.84); two-sided vs one-sided -> ~1.25x n. Also n explodes as baseline approaches 50% (variance peaks).

flashcards.q: Why does peeking invalidate fixed-horizon tests and how bad does it get?
flashcards.a: Fixed-horizon guarantees type-I error for exactly ONE look; repeated checks stop on inevitable random crossings, pushing realized false-positive rates from nominal 5% into the 20-40% range depending on check frequency.

flashcards.q: Name the three production-grade fixes for peeking.
flashcards.a: Group-sequential alpha-spending boundaries declared upfront (early looks demand extreme z-scores, e.g., |z|>3.9 where fixed-horizon needs 1.96); anytime-valid mSPRT p-values valid under arbitrary stopping; Bayesian monitoring on P(B>A)/expected-loss thresholds.

flashcards.q: What are novelty/primacy effects and the standard defenses?
flashcards.a: Week-1 effects partly reflect changed-ness (novelty) or delayed habit formation (primacy), decaying over time. Defenses: read after >=2 full weekly cycles; segment new vs returning users (novelty lives in returners); keep 1-5% long-term holdouts for cumulative portfolio truth.

flashcards.q: How do you report a null result correctly?
flashcards.a: Never 'no effect' - state achieved MDE: 'powered to rule out effects larger than ~X%'. Check realized variance vs assumptions, segments, and dilution (a +40% effect on an 8%-of-sessions surface reads ~+3.2% overall). Rerun bigger only if a revised MDE would still change the decision.

flashcards.q: 20 metrics tested at alpha=.05 with no correction: chance of at least one false positive?
flashcards.a: ~64% (1-(0.95)^20). Fix: pre-declared OEC, Bonferroni/Benjamini-Hochberg for exploratory reads, and explicit 'hypothesis-generating' labels on everything else.

flashcards.q: What is metric dilution and how do you analyze around it?
flashcards.a: A headline metric averaged over all users when only a fraction encounter the surface: true +40% on encounters dilutes to ~+3.2% if only 8% see it. Analyze triggered populations (users who actually reached the feature) while checking for selection artifacts.

flashcards.q: When must you cluster-randomize instead of user-randomize?
flashcards.a: Whenever spillover exists: referral/social features leak treated behavior into control arms (diluting estimates toward zero); marketplaces have cross-side equilibrium shifts (use geo switchbacks). The unit must match where the effect stabilizes without leaking.

flashcards.q: State Twyman's Law and its practical use.
flashcards.a: Any figure that looks unusual or interesting is usually wrong. A +200% lift is an instrumentation bug, segment flip, SRM artifact, or novelty burst until audited against raw event counts, arm composition, and logging joins. Minutes of audit vs shipping phantom wins.

flashcards.q: ~What fraction of ideas beat control at mature experimentation shops?
flashcards.a: Roughly 10-33% (Microsoft-era analyses, Booking.com's published experience). A team winning 80% of tests isn't talented - it's uncalibrated, testing only safe trivialities that don't need testing.
